background.definition: Acne is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis that is notable for open and closed comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) and inflammatory lesions including papules, pustules, cysts, and nodules.

list.listitem: Estimated 50 million people in the United States.
Roughly 85% of teenagers are affected; 12% prevalence in adult women.
In a cohort of 48,665 German adults (52% male), the prevalence of acne vulgaris by fairly strict criteria was 2.1%.
Estimated $100 million per year on over-the-counter medications.
Direct cost may exceed $3 billion each year in the United States.
Significant short- and long-term psychological and social implications for those affected due to the presence of acne lesions and scarring.

Skin conditions contributed 1.79% to the global burden of disease measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) from 306 diseases and injuries in 2013. Skin and subcutaneous diseases were the 18th leading cause of global DALYs in Global Burden of Disease 2013. Excluding mortality, skin diseases were the fourth leading cause of disability worldwide.
Alteration in balance of the androgen/estrogen axis.
Increase in androgen secretion leads to an increase in the size and activity of the pilosebaceous unit.

Precipitating or contributing factors include endocrine disorders, exogenous corticosteroids, antiepileptic medications, lithium, isoniazid, mechanical occlusion of the follicle with cosmetics or other topical products, and psychological stress.
Cow's milk and chocolate intake also appear to be associated with an increased risk of acne.
Excessive sebum production resulting from sebaceous gland hyperplasia primarily due to increases in androgenic hormones.
Hyperkeratinization of the hair follicle, which eventually plugs the follicular outflow tract, with subsequent accumulation of lipids and cellular debris.
Colonization of the follicle by Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), which causes an immune response.
Eventual rupture of the follicle, spilling lipids, debris, bacteria, and fatty acids into the surrounding dermis.
Diagnosis is based on the morphology of the lesions. Comedonal acne is primarily obstructive, while inflammatory acne has papules, pustules, nodules, and cysts. C
Routine microbiological testing of lesions is not necessary. B
Routine endocrinologic testing is not necessary. B

Characterized by burrowing and interconnecting abcesses and irregular scars

Keloid-like papules and plaques on occipital scalp exclusively in African Americans

list.listitem: Comedonal acne (acne comedonicus): characterized by many open or obstructed comedos, but scant inflammatory changes (see ).
Common acne (acne vulgaris) or pustular acne: characterized by pustules and comedos.
Cystic acne (acne cystica): patients have cystic foci of infection that result in scars.
Acne conglobata: multilobular inflammatory cysts containing volatile pus; therapy-resistant, scar forming.

Acne fulminans: an uncommon variant of acne in young men characterized by systemic symptoms (fever, arthralgia, skeletal foci of inflammation). Systemic corticosteroids plus isotretinoin, not antibiotics, are the drugs of choice. Refer patients with suspected acne fulminans to a dermatologist without delay. This painful disease is not well known and is often left untreated for a long time.
In women who are overweight, hirsute, and have irregular menses, consider polycystic ovary disease.
No testing needed because acne is a visual diagnosis based on the morphology of acne lesions.
Biopsies and cultures are not routinely recommended unless systemic infection is suspected.
See for diagnosis by type of acne.
Distinguish between comedonal and inflammatory acne first, and then determine severity. All acne types that are not primarily comedonal are inflammatory.
Severity is usually graded as mild, moderate, or severe. Comedonal acne is generally more mild than inflammatory acne, but widespread comedonal acne can be graded as moderate or severe.
The more nodules and cysts present, the greater the severity in all types of inflammatory acne.
Topical retinoids (eg, tretinoin, adapalene, and tazarotene) are effective in acne treatment and are especially useful in preventing comedones and new acne lesions. A
For mild to moderate inflammatory acne, combination topical agents (eg, adapalene/benzoyl peroxide, or clindamymcin/benzoyl peroxide) may be more effective than topical monotherapy. A
Benzoyl peroxide (any strength but lower strengths cause less irritation), as monotherapy or add-on therapy, appears more effective than no treatment or placebo for the management of acne. A

Oral antibiotics (tetracyclines and erythromycin) used alone or in combination with topical agents are the standard of care in the management of moderate to severe inflammatory acne and are especially needed for acne on the back and chest. A
Oral tetracycline, minocycline, doxycycline, and lymecycline appear similarly effective for the treatment of moderate to severe inflammatory acne. A
Isotretinoin is the recommended treatment for cystic and scarring acne that has not responded to other therapies. A
See for treatment by type of acne.
The UK NICE guidance provides a useful visual summary for clinicians.
Topical therapy is the first step in the treatment of mild acne.

Topical retinoids (eg, tretinoin, adapalene, and tazarotene) are effective in acne treatment and are especially useful in preventing comedones and new acne lesions. Adapalene and tretinoin are equally effective, and adapalene is less irritating than tretinoin. Dapsone 5% gel is more effective than placebo in treatment of acne vulgaris (NNT = 13).

Benzoyl peroxide (BPO), as monotherapy or add-on therapy, appears more effective than no treatment or placebo for the management of acne. As monotherapy, it appears as effective as topical adapalene or topical clindamycin. BPO is effective at various strengths to treat mild to moderate acne, however, higher concentrations (esp 10%) cause more irritation. BPO, in combination with topical antibiotics like erythromycin or clindamycin, is effective and has the theoretical advantage of preventing antimicrobial resistance of C. acnes.

For patients with mild to moderate acne, a 2021 network meta-analysis suggests the highest efficacy for combination topical therapies using adapalene plus BPO (odds ratio [OR] 3.65; 95% CI 2.58 - 5.15), followed by clindamycin plus BPO (OR 2.98; 2.22 - 4.01). Monotherapy with adapalene appears to be the third most effective topical treatment (OR 2.44; 1.66 - 3.60). Patients seem to tolerate adapelene alone when they do not tolerate BPO contaning combinations.
Azelaic acid is a unique agent that can be used to treat spotty hyperpigmentation and acne. As monotherapy, azelaic acid appears less effective than BPO, but comparable to topical tretinoin.
Topical 2% ketoconazole cream monotherapy significantly improved mild adult female acne in a double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial.

Based on two industry-funded phase 3 trials involving 1440 patients 9 years and older with moderate (83%) to severe (17%) acne, the anti-androgenic clascoterone 1% cream applied twice daily for 12 weeks appears more effective than placebo (vehicle cream) in achieving the primary outcome. This was defined as a 2-point decrease in the Investigator's Global Assessment score (range of 0 for clear to 4 for severe), and an overall assessment of clear (0) or almost clear (1). Study 1 favored the treatment group (18.4% vs 9.0%; P < .001; NNT = 11), as did Study 2 (20.3% vs 6.5%; P < .001; NNT = 7). Overall, the cream was well-tolerated and safe. In 2020, clascoterone received FDA approval for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 12 years and older. A 60 gram tube costs around $450 (goodrx.com, 11/2022).

Olumacostat glasaretil, a novel topical sebum inhibitor, demonstrated efficacy in treating acne vulgaris in a phase IIa, multicenter, randomized, vehicle-controlled trial; however, more studies need to be done.

An RCT of 181 patients found once weekly topical use of a powdered mixture of a freshwater sponge (Spongilla lacustris) to be effective in reducing inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions in patients 12 years and older with moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris.

Oral antibiotics (ie, tetracyclines and erythromycin) are the standard of care in the management of moderate to severe inflammatory acne and are especially needed for acne on the back and chest. Doxycycline, tetracycline, and minocycline are all effective. Minocycline is expensive (with increased risk of lupus-like syndrome) and appears no better than other systemic antibiotics including tetracycline.
Low-dose doxycycline (20 mg twice a day) is somewhat effective for moderate acne and may be considered for patients not able to tolerate higher doses.

Oral isotretinoin is the most powerful treatment for cystic and scarring acne that has not responded to other therapies. It is highly effective, but has significant adverse effects and is a known teratogen. Women of childbearing age must use two forms of contraception and be monitored for pregnancy monthly. Monitor all persons using isotretinoin for depression and order monthly lab tests to monitor for other side effects in select patients. Evidence from one systematic review did not support monthly laboratory monitoring in standard patients with acne on standard doses of isotretinoin.

A 2018 Cochrane review evaluating 31 RCTs, based on very low-quality evidence, found oral isotretinoin to be no better than oral antibiotics plus topical agents in improving acne severity based on trial investigator-assessed lesion count, but isotretinoin may be better at improving physician-assessed global evaluation.

A large network meta-analysis of 210 studies involving 65,601 patients found oral isotretinoin to be the most effective treatment for acne in terms of decreasing overall lesion count (48% relative reduction) and for decreasing inflammatory lesions (54% relative reduction). As far as treatment success using investigators' assessment, combination therapy with topical BPO and retinoids plus oral or topical antibiotics appears as effective as oral isotretinoin.

A systematic review of 11 trials with 760 randomized patients (mostly men, mean age 18 to 48 years) evaluated harms of isotretinoin. The rate of any adverse events was high (751 events), with 12 withdrawing from trials due to more serious harms such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), photophobia, depressed mood, headache, worsening of acne, elevated hepatic transaminases, xerosis, and cheilitis. The 2018 Cochrane review only reported one serious adverse event (SJS) among 400 participants, but found 67% higher risk of minor adverse events (dry lips/skin, cheilitis, vomiting, nausea).
Prescribers of isotretinoin, patients who take isotretinoin, and pharmacists who dispense isotretinoin must register with the iPLEDGE system (http://www.ipledgeprogram.com).

ACOG guidelines have pointed to the role of triphasic, combination oral contraceptives (eg, norgestimate-ethinyl estradiol) in the treatment of moderate acne in women without contraindications to oral contraceptives.
Combined oral contraceptives appear effective in treating comedonal and inflammatory acne.
Oral contraceptives with an antiandrogenic progestin derivative may be slightly more effective than other oral contraceptives in improving mild to moderate acne.

A meta-analysis comparing efficacy of antibiotics and oral contraceptive compared with placebo at 3 and 6 months showed antibiotics were superior at 3 months but oral contraceptives are equivalent to antibiotics at 6 months in reducing acne lesions.

Oral antiandrogens such as spironolactone are occasionally used in adult women for the treatment of acne when other methods fail. However, clinical trial evidence is limited, and comparisons between spironolactone and oral contraceptives have not demonstrated that one is more effective or safer than the other.
Metformin and OCPs had similar impact on hirsutism in PCOS patients.

Anti-inflammatory dose oral doxycycline (40mg) plus adapalene 0.3% and benzoyl peroxide 2.5% gel lead to significant improvements in Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA) scores for patients with severe acne.
Nodulocystic lesions may acutely improve with intralesional injections of dilute triamcinolone acetonide.
Be careful to avoid skin atrophy by not using too much steroid per injection. Dilutions of triamcinolone acetonide at 2 mg/mL may be used with a injection volume of 0.1 mL per lesion.

Polymethylmethacrylate microspheres in collagen (ArteFill) were shown in a masked RCT to be more effective than saline injections for treatment of facial acne scars (64% vs 33% treatment success, p = 0.0005, NNT = 3).

A 2016 Cochrane review found moderate-quality evidence of short-term improvement in atrophic acne scars with injectable fillers, but concluded that long-term, placebo-controlled (or sham) trials are needed.
A small split-face masked RCT in 20 patients found that a dermal rolling needle device may also be effective for treatment of acne scars.
Oral and external herbal extracts described in ayurvedic medicine have been used to treat acne.Studies are of limited quality and do not compare these herbal therapies with Western treatments.

A 2015 Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that tea tree oil, bee venom, and low-glycemic-load-diet may decrease the number of acne lesions. Insufficient evidence was found for herbal medicine, acupuncture, and wet-cupping. Potential adverse events need to be considered when using herbal medicine with traditional drugs.
Pulsed dye laser was found to be no more effective than watchful waiting.
Chemical peels are used to treat acne scars. Data are lacking, and the cost may be prohibitive.

Intense pulsed light (IPL) and photodynamic therapy (PDT) use lasers, special lights, and topical chemicals to treat acne. While these methods may work, no data suggest that they work better than other methods when used alone, and they are expensive. A 2016 Cochrane review failed to identify high-quality evidence to support the use of light therapies for acne.
An RCT evaluating 95 patients with moderate to severe facial acne found PDT plus oral minocycline more effective than minocycline monotherapy in improving acne symptoms and quality of life (QOL).
A novel topical minocycline foam has shown to reduce both inflammatory and noninflammatory lesions and improved global assessment scores in moderate to severe acne.
Studies of facial cleansing and increased ultraviolet exposure reveal mixed results, but some small randomized trials have shown a benefit of these interventions.

Chocolate does make acne worse based on a randomized crossover study with statistically significant increase in acne lesion in chocolate consumption group compared to jelly beans (+4.8 vs −0.7 lesions respectively). Skim milk more than whole milk appears to be associated with a slightly increased risk of teenage acne.
Internet based education using automated counseling was not superior to standard website education in improving acne severity and QOL.
Microneedling may improve scarring from acne, but further studies are warranted.
Significant improvement may take 1 month or longer after initiating treatment.
There is insufficient data to guide optimal dosing of tetracycline antibiotics.
Refer patients with severe refractory nodulocystic acne requiring isotretinoin therapy to a dermatologist or physician experienced with isotretinoin therapy.
Refer cases of acne fulminans and acne conglobata to a dermatologist.
Prognosis varies; however, successful treatment is based on the patient's perception. C
Waxing and waning disease course is typical, but clinical improvement and even resolution may occur beyond adolescence and early adulthood. C
Follow up as needed based on patient's feedback. C
Isotretinoin and tazarotene are category X and should never be used in pregnancy. Order pregnancy tests before and during use in women of childbearing potential.
Erythromycin (topical or oral) and azelaic acid are category B, and there is no evidence of second or third trimester harm.
Avoid all topical retinoids; topical tretinoin is category C.
Benzoyl peroxide is also category C.

feature.caption: Treatment by Type of Acne.
feature.feature_body:
Type of Acne Initial Treatment Second-Line Treatment
Comedonal Keratolyticsa Add benzoyl peroxide if necessary
Papulopustular Keratolyticsa PLUS benzoyl peroxide PLUS topical antibioticb Add systemic antibiotic if necessaryc
Nodulocystic Keratolyticsa PLUS benzoyl peroxide PLUS topical antibioticb PLUS systemic antibioticc Consider isotretinoin in severe refractory cases; oral contraceptive pills and/or spironolactone in women; and intralesional steroids
Acne conglobata and acne fulminans Oral prednisone and oral isotretinoin Add intralesional steroids for rapid therapy of painful lesions
aKeratolytics include topical tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene, and azelaic acid. bTopical antibiotics include erythromycin and clindamycin. cSystemic antibiotics include doxycycline, tetracycline, minocycline, and erythromycin.
